summary.text: 送 means ‘send’ or ‘see someone off.’ Its standard form has 辶, the side form of 辵 ‘walk,’ beside an element analyzed as 灷 in one account and as reduced 㑞 in another. The gift-carrying image is a mnemonic, not an established ancient picture.

formation.text: A probable phonosemantic compound: 辵 contributes walking or going, and one analysis assigns 灷 a phonetic role. Shuowen instead analyzes the graph as 辵 plus a reduced 㑞. The historical sound comparison for 灷 is unavailable in this evidence.

components.text: The visible 辶 is the conventional side form of 辵, associated here with walking or going. It is a positional form, not a later replacement.

One analysis identifies 灷 as the sound element. It describes a bronze form as 廾 with 丨 and decorative dots, and reports a graphic alteration in small-seal writing. Shuowen instead identifies reduced 㑞; how the analyses relate remains unresolved.

sound_limitation.text: No historical reading for 灷 is supplied for comparison with 送. The modern Mandarin readings zhuàn and sòng do not establish an ancient sound relation; the supplied Old Chinese reconstruction is for 送 alone.

sound.text: Modern Mandarin readings are zhuàn for 灷 and sòng for 送; this is a comparison of current readings only.

history.text: Shuowen glosses 送 as 遣 and analyzes it as 辵 plus reduced 㑞. It also records a fuller Zhou-script form, 𨕼. This historical dictionary analysis differs from the bronze-form analysis identifying 灷.

Another analysis describes a bronze form as 辵 plus 灷 and reports a graphic alteration of 灷 in small-seal writing. Discussions of Chu-slip forms propose several possible shape pathways and caution that at least one form cannot be placed in a simple sequence by shape alone; the graphic history remains unresolved.
In the standard graph, 辵 appears in its positional form 辶. This explains the visible side shape but does not date the word or its meanings.

A graph in one Zhongshan inscription has been read as 朕, ‘I, my.’ This specific inscriptional reading does not establish that 送 was generally borrowed to write the pronoun or identify the name or pronunciation of a depicted object.

uncertainties.text: The analyses differ over whether the second element is 灷 or reduced 㑞. The phonetic role assigned to 灷 lacks an independently demonstrated historical sound comparison with 送.
The available form discussions do not settle a single graphic sequence or precisely date the earliest surviving form of 送.

The reading 朕 applies to a graph in one inscription; a general phonetic-loan history is not established, and the evidence does not identify an object's name or ancient pronunciation behind that reading.

senses.period: early received Shijing text; composition date unresolved
senses.text: A received poem uses 送 in a context interpreted as accompanying someone to a place. It attests an early accompanying or sending context, without settling the precise distinction between accompanying and seeing someone off.

senses.period: Han-dynasty lexicographic record and medieval dictionary record
senses.text: Shuowen glosses 送 as 遣; a medieval dictionary record gives the same gloss and a fanqie reading. These records attest the gloss in those dictionaries, not when the sense began.
A supplied modern definition includes ‘give,’ but no dated usage here establishes when this use arose or how it relates to sending.

developments.text: The senses are compatible with a broader sending meaning, but no dated transition or semantic development between them is established.
The modern gloss ‘give’ is supplied without dated evidence establishing when or how it relates to sending or dispatching.

limitations.text: The received-text quotation does not establish the poem’s composition date or priority among accompanying, seeing off, and sending senses. Dictionary gloss order does not establish semantic chronology.

overview.text: 送 means ‘send’ or ‘see someone off.’ Its form combines 辶, associated with walking, with 灷, which one analysis assigns a sound role; a historical pronunciation comparison is unavailable here. The gift-carrying image is a mnemonic.

components.text: 辶 is the side form of 辵, associated with walking, and contributes the idea of going here.
One analysis assigns 灷 a sound role, but the historical pronunciation comparison is unavailable here.

relationships.text: In 送, 辶 is the positional form of 辵 and contributes the walking or going sense.

One analysis assigns 灷 a phonetic role in 送. Modern Mandarin readings are zhuàn and sòng, but no historical sound correspondence is independently demonstrated; the supplied Old Chinese reconstruction is for 送 alone.
